stories.headline: Energy Department Issues Emergency Orders for Mid-Atlantic Power Grid Amid Dangerous Heat Wave
stories.summary:
The Trump administration's Energy Department issued emergency orders Wednesday directing grid operator PJM to maximize power output from fossil fuel plants, bypassing normal environmental restrictions, as a dangerous heat dome descends on the East Coast and Midwest. Energy Secretary Chris Wright authorized the emergency measures in response to warnings from PJM of potential power shortages across a region serving tens of millions of Americans.

The National Weather Service warned that more than 175 million Americans will face major or extreme heat risk by Friday, with hundreds of cities potentially setting all-time temperature records. The emergency orders allow fossil fuel plants that would ordinarily be subject to emissions limits to operate at full capacity to meet surging electricity demand.

The move reflects the administration's broader posture of prioritizing energy reliability over environmental constraints during crisis conditions. Critics of such emergency waivers argue they set a precedent for sidelining emissions rules, while supporters contend grid stability and public safety must take priority when lives are at risk from extreme heat.

stories.headline: Zelensky Warns of Imminent Massive Russian Strike as Kyiv Absorbs Overnight Missile and Drone Attack
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Wednesday that Russia has been preparing a massive strike against Ukraine, hours after Kyiv was hit by a barrage of Russian ballistic missiles and drones overnight. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed multiple explosions across the capital, with at least two people killed and eleven injured as Ukrainian air defenses worked to intercept incoming projectiles.

Zelensky issued the warning on social media, framing the overnight attack as a prelude to a larger planned offensive by Vladimir Putin. The strikes came amid an active period of cross-border attacks, including a Ukrainian drone strike that recently hit a major communications center in Moscow.

The escalation underscores continued instability in the war despite ongoing diplomatic contacts. Zelensky's public warning of a coming massive strike is notable for its specificity, suggesting Ukrainian intelligence has detected Russian preparations, and raises concerns about the scale of potential civilian casualties if the anticipated offensive materializes.

stories.headline: McConnell Was Found Unconscious at Home Last Month; Condition and Return to Senate Remain Unknown
stories.summary:
Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., was found unconscious at his Washington, D.C. home on June 14 before being transported to the hospital, according to emergency dispatch audio released Wednesday by reporter Desirée Townsend and subsequently reported by PunchBowl News. The dispatch recording revealed that an Advanced Life Support response was requested, a detail that McConnell's office had not previously disclosed when it announced his hospitalization that day.

McConnell, 82, has not returned to the Senate since the incident, and his office has declined to comment on his condition, the cause of hospitalization, or a timeline for his return. His spokesperson had said only that McConnell was "receiving excellent care" and was "working closely with staff on Senate business." Senate Majority Leader John Thune said McConnell is "clearly dialed in" and following Senate activity.

The revelation intensifies scrutiny of McConnell's health at a critical legislative moment. It is his second hospitalization of 2026, following an eight-day stay in February for flu-like symptoms, and comes amid a pattern of public medical episodes dating to 2023 that included falls, a concussion, and on-camera freezing episodes. McConnell is retiring from the Senate at the end of this year.

stories.headline: DOJ Charges Eight Tren de Aragua Members With Kidnapping and Murder of Americans in Texas and Illinois
stories.summary:
The Department of Justice announced Wednesday the indictment of eight members of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua on charges including kidnapping and murder of American citizens, including children, in Texas and Illinois. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, joined by FBI Director Kash Patel and two U.S. attorneys, announced the charges at a press conference, providing graphic details of the alleged crimes.

In one case outside Dallas in 2024, four men allegedly murdered a father and kidnapped his 13-year-old daughter and 12-year-old nephew. In a separate Chicago case less than two months ago, a man was allegedly kidnapped in broad daylight, bound, transported to an abandoned building, shot multiple times, and left dead. Blanche stated all eight defendants entered the country between December 2021 and April 2024, blaming the Biden administration for their entry.

Patel reported a 519% increase in Tren de Aragua arrests since the start of Trump's second term, with nearly 350 members charged or convicted overall and 29,000 total violent gang members arrested. The announcement reflects the administration's emphasis on gang enforcement as a centerpiece of its immigration and public safety agenda. Critics have raised due process concerns about the administration's broad application of terrorism designations, while supporters argue aggressive prosecution is necessary to protect American communities.

stories.headline: Update: Nigeria Demands Compensation as South Africa Anti-Migrant Crisis Escalates After Deadline
stories.summary:
Nigeria announced it will seek compensation from South Africa for property and businesses abandoned by Nigerian citizens who fled anti-migrant violence, marking a significant diplomatic escalation. Nigeria's acting High Commissioner to South Africa said the government has begun documenting assets left behind, while more than 600 Nigerians have already been repatriated and hundreds more await evacuation flights.

The development follows the expiration of a June 30 deadline set by anti-migrant groups demanding undocumented foreigners leave South Africa. Marches on Tuesday were largely peaceful but included isolated violence against foreigners; South African police reported approximately 900 arrests, mostly for immigration-related offenses and looting. About 25,000 nationals from other African countries have left South Africa in recent weeks.

Nigeria's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said all compensation claims would be verified before any formal request is made and that diplomatic ties have not been severed. South Africa's government has not yet responded to the compensation demand. The dispute reflects broader regional tensions over migration policy and the safety of African nationals living across the continent.

One Nigerian trader awaiting repatriation told the BBC he had lived in South Africa for nearly a decade, abandoned his clothing business in Centurion, and estimated goods left behind were worth more than 16,000 rand. He expressed doubt he would ever receive compensation, saying: "If South Africa government can compensate it, it will be nice, but I know they won't."

stories.headline: Syria Names Final 70 Lawmakers to New Post-Assad Parliament Ahead of First Session
stories.summary:
Syrian Interim President Ahmed al-Sharaa has appointed the final 70 members of the country's new 210-seat People's Assembly, completing the legislature's formation ahead of its inaugural session next week. Fifteen of the new appointees are women and 13 were imprisoned under the rule of ousted President Bashar al-Assad, who was overthrown in 2024.

Two-thirds of the assembly were selected last October through regional electoral colleges, but that process drew criticism after only six seats went to women and ten to minority candidates. Officials said Sharaa would use his presidential appointments to address the imbalance. The final slate includes relatives of those killed in the civil war, survivors of detention and chemical attacks, academics, and community leaders drawn from all 14 Syrian provinces.

The assembly formation has faced significant controversy. More than 20 Kurdish parties rejected lawmakers selected in northern provinces, citing "exclusion and marginalisation," and fourteen Syrian civil society groups criticized the electoral system as structurally flawed, warning that the president's broad powers over committee membership and appointments could allow him to dominate a body meant to be independent. Elections have not yet been held in the predominantly Druze province of Suweida due to ongoing instability.

The UN deputy special envoy last week told the Security Council that Syria's transition is "at a critical phase, with opportunity," underscoring the international community's close watch on whether the new parliament can serve as a genuine check on executive power in the fragile post-war state.

stories.headline: Trial Opens for Maltese Businessman Accused in 2017 Car Bomb Murder of Journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia
stories.summary:
Maltese businessman Yorgen Fenech, 44, went on trial in Valletta on Wednesday on charges of complicity in the 2017 car bomb assassination of prominent investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. A jury was sworn in for the high-profile case, which is expected to last several weeks. Fenech has denied all charges.

Caruana Galizia was a prominent critic of Malta's government who had exposed corruption networks in Malta and abroad before her killing. Brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio were jailed for 40 years in 2022 for carrying out the murder, and two other men received life sentences in 2025 for supplying the bomb. A fifth man secured a pardon in exchange for testimony.

Fenech faces charges of complicity in voluntary homicide and criminal association with intent to commit murder. Members of Caruana Galizia's family, including her three sons, were present in the courtroom to witness the start of proceedings. Her assassination shocked Malta and prompted widespread protests over press freedom and government accountability.

The case carries significance beyond Malta's borders as a test of whether powerful business figures can be held accountable for attacks on journalists. Fenech's trial is the culmination of one of the most complex and politically sensitive criminal investigations in the country's history.

stories.headline: German Prosecutors Charge Ukrainian National Over 2022 Nord Stream Pipeline Bombings
stories.summary:
German federal prosecutors have filed formal charges against a Ukrainian national identified as Serhii K. over the September 2022 sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines beneath the Baltic Sea. The suspect is accused of leading and coordinating a seven-person team that destroyed three of the four pipelines, which transported Russian natural gas to Germany. He was arrested in Italy in 2024, extradited to Germany in November, and has denied involvement. A second Ukrainian suspect was detained near Warsaw on a separate German arrest warrant.

The charges include leading a criminal attack on civil energy infrastructure, causing explosions, and destroying infrastructure. The blasts released record amounts of methane into the Baltic Sea and rendered the multi-billion-dollar pipeline network inoperable. No government or group has claimed responsibility for the attack, and Ukraine has officially denied involvement.

The prosecution carries significant diplomatic weight. Germany is Ukraine's largest European military aid provider, and many Ukrainians view the Nord Stream destruction as a patriotic act that cut off a key Russian revenue source, complicating public and political acceptance of the prosecution in both countries. Russia, the United States, and United Kingdom have all been named in various theories, but no state link has been established by investigators.

The case represents the first formal criminal prosecution connected to one of the most consequential acts of infrastructure sabotage in modern European history. The outcome could affect Germany-Ukraine relations and reopen international debate over accountability for the attack.

stories.headline: Greek Politician's Mother Dies After Coordinated Arson Attacks Target Ruling Party Officials in Thessaloniki
stories.summary:
Vagia Nestora, 72, the mother of a New Democracy party candidate in Greece, died Wednesday of burns covering approximately 80 percent of her body sustained in one of three coordinated arson attacks targeting ruling party officials in Thessaloniki. The attacks occurred within minutes of each other in the early hours of Wednesday morning, with improvised incendiary devices placed outside three separate apartment buildings linked to New Democracy politicians. Her daughter Afroditi Nestora, the party candidate who lived at the targeted address, remains hospitalized with burns and smoke inhalation.

Two other attacks struck the homes of the chairman of New Democracy's Thessaloniki administrative committee and a former New Democracy member of parliament, causing property damage but no additional injuries. Police believe all three attacks were carried out by the same perpetrators traveling by motorcycle. Greece's Counter-Terrorism Service has taken over the investigation and no arrests have been made.

Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis condemned the killing as an act of terrorism, saying it exposed the "murderous and inhumane nature" of political violence and called for a unified national response. Opposition leader Nikos Androulakis and former Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras also condemned the attack, with Tsipras stating that "terrorism has no place in a democracy."

No group has claimed responsibility. Greece has a history of far-left domestic extremist groups carrying out attacks on politicians and public figures, though investigators have not publicly identified any suspects or attributed the attacks to a specific organization.

stories.headline: House Democrats Sound Alarm After Socialist Challenger Defeats Rep. Diana DeGette in Colorado Primary
stories.summary:
House Democrats erupted in anxiety and anger Wednesday following the primary defeat of Rep. Diana DeGette of Colorado, a long-serving and reliably progressive member, at the hands of a democratic socialist challenger. The loss came a day after the Democratic Socialists of America posted multiple upsets in New York primaries, including the defeat of Rep. Dan Goldman, accelerating what party insiders describe as a destabilizing internal civil war. DeGette's defeat in particular rattled members who noted she was not a moderate — raising fears that no incumbent is safe from a left-primary challenge regardless of their ideological record.

Senior House Democrats, speaking anonymously to Axios, described the results as a "wake up call" and criticized what one member called "the growing dynamic of performative politics." The defeats have deepened a rift between the party's establishment wing and its progressive base at a moment when Democrats are seeking to present a unified opposition to the Trump administration.

The string of socialist primary victories reflects a broader realignment on the Democratic left, where grassroots energy and small-dollar fundraising have increasingly favored candidates running explicitly against the party's incumbent class. Progressive leaders such as Zohran Mamdani, who won the New York mayoral primary, have argued that the party must embrace a more confrontational posture on economic issues to energize voters.

Establishment Democrats and some moderate strategists counter that socialist-branded candidates will struggle in general elections in competitive districts, potentially handing Republicans seats the party needs to retake the House. The tension mirrors debates within the party dating to the 2018 and 2020 cycles but is intensifying as primaries continue into summer.

stories.headline: Update: Venezuela Earthquake Death Toll Surpasses 1,900 as Trump Administration Attacks Opposition Leader Machado Over Return Attempts
stories.summary:
One week after twin earthquakes devastated Venezuela on June 24, the confirmed death toll has surpassed 1,900 with tens of thousands still reported missing, according to new figures cited Wednesday. The disaster has unfolded against a politically charged backdrop as Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has made repeated high-profile attempts to return to the country from exile amid the crisis.

Senior Trump administration officials have sharply criticized Machado's efforts, with one official calling her conduct "political opportunism" and describing it as "grotesque." A State Department official said her maneuvers have saddled U.S. diplomats with "extra needless drama" at a moment when Washington is engaged in relief coordination efforts in Venezuela, warning that her actions risk inflaming political tensions and complicating the U.S.-assisted humanitarian response.

Machado, the most prominent face of Venezuela's opposition movement, has argued that a national disaster requires her physical presence in the country to organize and advocate for affected communities. Her supporters contend the Trump administration's criticism reflects discomfort with her independent political profile even as Washington positions itself as a humanitarian actor in the crisis.

The rebuke represents a notable moment of friction between the Trump administration and a foreign opposition leader Washington has previously praised. It underscores the complexity of U.S. policy toward Venezuela, where the administration has pursued a mix of sanctions pressure, diplomatic engagement, and now disaster relief, with Nicolás Maduro's government still in power.

stories.headline: Defiant Catholic Traditionalists Ordain Four Bishops as Pope Warns of Schism
stories.summary:
Thousands gathered in Écône, Switzerland on Wednesday as the Society of Saint Pius X ordained four new Catholic bishops in direct defiance of Pope Leo XIV, who had issued a last-minute appeal calling the act a "schismatic act" that could "tear the seamless garment of Christ." The four new bishops hail from the United States, Switzerland, and France. The society rejects key modernizing reforms introduced by the Vatican in the 1960s and 1970s, including permission to celebrate Mass in vernacular languages rather than Latin.

The SSPX, founded by French Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre in 1970, has long resisted Vatican directives on interfaith dialogue, religious freedom, and liturgical reform. At least 15,000 attendees witnessed the ceremony, conducted entirely in Latin. The last time the society ordained bishops without papal consent, in 1988, they were immediately excommunicated; Pope Benedict XVI repealed those excommunications in 2009 in an unsuccessful bid to heal the rift.

Pope Leo XIV is expected to excommunicate the four newly ordained bishops, deepening the most significant formal rupture within Roman Catholicism in decades. The episode illustrates enduring tensions between traditionalist Catholic movements and the post-Vatican II church, with SSPX leaders insisting the ordinations were an act of fidelity rather than rebellion. The Vatican views unauthorized episcopal ordinations as a fundamental violation of church unity and papal authority.

stories.headline: Phil Weiser Upsets Michael Bennet to Win Colorado Democratic Gubernatorial Primary
stories.summary:
Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser defeated incumbent U.S. Senator Michael Bennet in Tuesday's Democratic primary for governor, a significant upset that highlighted voter frustration with Washington-based political figures. Bennet, who has served in the Senate for 17 years, was considered a high-profile establishment candidate, while Weiser positioned himself as a state-focused fighter better aligned with the concerns of Colorado voters.

Democrats have dominated Colorado statewide races for more than a decade, making Weiser the early favorite heading into the November general election. The result signals a broader appetite within the Democratic Party for candidates rooted in state government rather than federal incumbents, a dynamic playing out in primaries across the country as the party debates its direction.

The primary outcome has national implications as Democrats assess which candidate profiles resonate in competitive states ahead of the 2026 midterms. Weiser's victory over a long-serving senator suggests that name recognition and federal experience alone may not be sufficient to energize a Democratic base seeking more combative, locally grounded leadership.

stories.headline: Dublin Stabbing Suspect Found Guilty on All Counts; Attack Sparked Worst Riots in Irish History
stories.summary:
Riad Bouchaker, 52, was found guilty Wednesday on all eight charges stemming from a November 2023 knife attack in Dublin's Parnell Square that left three children seriously injured and a crèche worker gravely hurt. A jury deliberated approximately six hours before returning unanimous verdicts. A five-year-old girl sustained a life-long brain injury after being stabbed in the heart; Bouchaker was also convicted of assaulting two other children and a teenager. Sentencing is scheduled for October 12.

The attack triggered the most serious riots in the history of the Irish state. Within hours, rioters destroyed 11 police vehicles, damaged or looted 13 shops, and burned three buses and a tram during three hours of sustained clashes. Ireland deployed its largest-ever number of riot police to restore order. Then-police chief Drew Harris attributed the unrest to what he called a "lunatic, hooligan faction driven by a far-right ideology."

The verdict closes a significant chapter in an episode that exposed deep social tensions in Ireland around immigration and public safety. The case drew sustained coverage across Europe and became a flashpoint in debates about far-right radicalization and the security implications of high-profile violent incidents in major cities.

stories.headline: Sony to End Physical Game Discs for PlayStation from January 2028
stories.summary:
Sony announced Wednesday that all new PlayStation game titles released from January 2028 onward will be distributed exclusively through digital channels, ending physical disc production for new releases. The company said digital downloads already account for approximately 80 percent of its full-game software sales in fiscal 2025, reflecting a years-long consumer shift away from physical media. Games already scheduled for disc release before that date will not be affected by the change.

Sony also announced it will begin shutting down the PlayStation Store on its legacy PS3 and PlayStation Vita consoles, starting in select markets in Latin America and the Middle East later this year and expanding globally in July 2027. The company cited the consoles' inability to support modern secure payment systems as the reason. Users will retain access to previously purchased content after the stores close.

The move marks a landmark transition for the gaming industry, where physical media has been a retail staple for decades. Critics and consumer advocates have raised concerns about digital-only distribution, including questions about game ownership, the inability to resell titles, and long-term access if digital storefronts are discontinued. The announcement is likely to accelerate similar considerations at other major gaming platform holders.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Strikes Down Trump Birthright Citizenship Order 5-4; Thomas Dissent Runs 91 Pages
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court ruled 5-4 Tuesday that the 14th Amendment guarantees birthright citizenship to children born in the United States, including those born to parents in the country illegally or on temporary visas, striking down President Trump's executive order that sought to deny such citizenship. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the majority opinion, holding that the order was not only unlawful but unconstitutional. The ruling is among the most significant immigration decisions in decades, directly affecting hundreds of thousands of births annually to noncitizen parents.

Justice Clarence Thomas authored a 91-page dissent arguing that the majority relied on 'alternative history' of the 14th Amendment and that its ruling 'devalues' citizenship. Thomas contended that the Citizenship Clause was designed for people with permanent domicile in the United States — freed slaves and their descendants — and that temporary visitors and those present illegally do not meet that standard under the amendment's original public meaning. He argued that many applications of the president's order were consistent with the clause as originally understood.

Supporters of the ruling say it reaffirms a foundational constitutional principle established after the Civil War and protects the citizenship status of millions of Americans born to immigrant parents. Supporters of Trump's position, including Thomas, argue the clause has been stretched far beyond its original intent and that Congress, not the courts, should define the scope of citizenship for children of noncitizens.

The decision ends a major legal battle that began when Trump signed the order among his first actions in office. It represents a significant defeat for the administration's immigration agenda, though the White House has not yet indicated whether it will seek any further legislative or constitutional avenue to revisit birthright citizenship policy.

stories.headline: U.S. Lifts Export Ban on Anthropic's Most Advanced AI Models After Security Agreement
stories.summary:
The U.S. Department of Commerce has lifted its export ban on Anthropic's two most advanced artificial intelligence models, Fable 5 and Mythos 5, just weeks after ordering the company to restrict global access over national security concerns. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick notified Anthropic that access would be restored beginning Wednesday, after the company agreed to proactively detect and address security risks and to alert the government of any malicious activity detected through its platforms.

The models were abruptly suspended on June 12 amid government concerns that they could be exploited by hackers to identify and attack vulnerabilities in computer systems. Anthropic had publicly disputed the breadth of the action, saying authorities had not identified specific concerns and that the discovery of a narrow potential jailbreak did not justify recalling tools deployed to hundreds of millions of users worldwide. Mythos 5 is specifically designed for businesses and cybersecurity professionals and is capable of identifying and exploiting vulnerabilities in code.

The reversal marks a notable shift in the government's posture and establishes a new precedent for how federal authorities may regulate advanced AI model releases — including reserved rights to reimpose restrictions if necessary. The agreement also requires Anthropic to collaborate with the government on future model releases, signaling an emerging regulatory framework for frontier AI systems with potential dual-use risks.

The episode highlights the growing tension between rapid commercial AI deployment and national security oversight, a debate that is accelerating as AI capabilities expand. Anthropic's Claude platform competes directly with OpenAI's ChatGPT and Google's Gemini in both consumer and enterprise markets.

stories.headline: Fire Kills at Least Six in Antwerp Apartment Block, Evacuates 80 Flats
stories.summary:
A fire broke out Wednesday morning in a ten-storey residential building in the Linkeroever district of Antwerp, Belgium, killing at least six people and injuring several others. Police said more than 200 people live in the block and that 80 flats were evacuated. Firefighters described a complex operation in which thick smoke spread rapidly through the building, severely hampering rescue and evacuation efforts.

Authorities said the fire was caused by a technical problem on the ground floor. Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever expressed condolences and the Flemish parliament opened its afternoon session with a moment of silence for the victims. The blaze was reported nearly under control by mid-afternoon, but emergency crews continued to search the building flat by flat for additional victims.

Dramatic footage circulated showing a resident climbing from his balcony through a neighbor's window to escape the smoke. One resident described barricading himself and waiting on a balcony until firefighters arrived with a ladder. The building's fire brigade spokeswoman said poor visibility made the response unusually difficult.

stories.headline: Three Die From Suffocation in Mexico City Crowds During World Cup Celebrations
stories.summary:
Three people died from suffocation Tuesday night during mass celebrations in Mexico City following the Mexican national football team's 2-0 victory over Ecuador in the FIFA World Cup. A 19-year-old woman, a 48-year-old woman, and a 44-year-old man were treated by emergency services at separate locations along Paseo de la Reforma before being transported to hospital, where all three were confirmed dead. City health authorities said more than one million people flooded the streets, primarily around the Angel of Independence monument.

City Mayor Clara Brugada expressed condolences to the victims' families and urged fans to 'celebrate with responsibility, care, and empathy.' She had warned before the match that crowds near the monument were already dangerously large and asked fans to find alternative viewing locations. Emergency services performed CPR on all three individuals before their transport to hospital.

The win marks Mexico's first World Cup knockout-stage victory since 1986 and sends the team into the round of 16. The scale of the celebration reflected the national significance of the result, though the deaths cast a shadow over the festivities. Mexico City's metropolitan area is home to more than 20 million people, making crowd management at major events a persistent public safety challenge.

stories.headline: Taliban Strike Pakistan in Retaliation as Afghanistan-Pakistan Border War Escalates
stories.summary:
Afghanistan's Taliban government launched retaliatory drone and missile strikes against targets in Pakistan's southwestern Balochistan province on Tuesday, injuring several people. Pakistan's military said it shot down four rudimentary drones and issued a warning that any further provocation would receive a "befitting response." The BBC has been unable to independently confirm all details of the strikes.

The exchange follows Pakistan's air strikes on Afghanistan on Sunday, which the United Nations said killed at least 28 civilians. Pakistan's information minister said the operation killed 29 militants in response to recent terrorist attacks on Pakistani soil. Afghanistan put the civilian death toll at 36, with more than 160 injured, describing the Pakistani attack as a "cowardly act" and an "atrocity."

The two nuclear-armed neighbors had agreed to a ceasefire in October following weeks of deadly clashes, but tensions have now reignited sharply. Pakistan accuses Afghanistan of harboring militants who carry out attacks on Pakistani territory; the Taliban government denies the charge and accuses Islamabad of unprovoked strikes on civilians. Earlier incidents this year include a March Pakistani strike on a Kabul drug rehabilitation center that killed hundreds.

The escalating cycle of cross-border strikes raises serious regional stability concerns. Both countries have civilian populations bearing the brunt of the violence, and with neither side showing signs of de-escalation, international observers warn the situation could deteriorate further.

stories.headline: Amnesty: Sudan's RSF Committed Crimes Against Humanity, Possible Genocide in El-Fasher
stories.summary:
Amnesty International released a major report Wednesday documenting crimes against humanity and ethnic cleansing committed by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces (RSF) during their 18-month siege and takeover of el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur. The report, based on accounts from more than 200 survivors and analysis of 89 open-source videos and extensive satellite imagery, says RSF crimes included murder, rape, sexual slavery, torture, enslavement, and the deliberate targeting of children. Amnesty's secretary general said evidence gathered "may be relevant to the crime of genocide."

The RSF, composed largely of Arab fighters, targeted members of non-Arab ethnic communities, frequently using ethnic slurs, according to the rights group. One 17-year-old survivor described being beaten with rifle stocks and shot in the leg; eight of his cousins, including four boys aged 11 to 17, were killed in the same attack. The RSF has not responded to the new report but has denied previous accusations of atrocities.

Sudan's civil war between the RSF and the regular Sudanese Armed Forces has now lasted three years, killing hundreds of thousands and displacing more than 14 million people. The UN has documented widespread sexual violence being used as a weapon of war by both sides, though both the RSF and the Sudanese Armed Forces deny the allegations against them.

The Amnesty report adds significant weight to calls for international accountability mechanisms. El-Fasher's fall was widely described as one of the bloodiest episodes of the conflict, and the new documentation of systematic ethnic targeting is likely to intensify pressure on the UN Security Council and the International Criminal Court to act.

stories.headline: DSA Wins New York Primary Races as Dan Goldman Loses Congressional Seat
stories.summary:
Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates scored significant victories in Tuesday's New York congressional primaries, with Darializa Avila Chevalier winning in the 10th Congressional District and additional DSA-aligned candidates prevailing in state-level races. Incumbent Rep. Dan Goldman, who served as lead counsel during the first Trump impeachment, lost his seat in the 10th District. Political strategist George Conway, a vocal Trump critic whose ex-wife Kellyanne Conway was a senior Trump adviser, also lost his primary bid in the 12th District.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, himself a democratic socialist elected last year, appeared at Avila Chevalier's victory party and called the results proof that his own victory was "not an anomaly." DSA local chapter co-chair Gustavo Gordillo declared the night validated a decade of movement-building, saying New Yorkers "want more socialist leadership." The results represent a notable leftward shift in New York's Democratic congressional delegation.

President Trump celebrated the results on social media, writing that Goldman "just lost, BIG" and accusing him of "illegally targeting President TRUMP." Trump also highlighted Conway's defeat. The outcomes fuel an ongoing intra-party debate within the Democratic Party over ideological direction, with progressive and democratic socialist factions arguing the results demonstrate a mandate for a harder left turn.

The primary outcomes could have implications for the general election in November, as the 10th and 12th Districts are reliably Democratic seats in New York City. Republicans in competitive upstate districts, meanwhile, are watching the leftward shift in the city's delegation as potential general-election fodder.

stories.headline: Beijing Plane Crash Into China's Tallest Skyscraper Shrouded in Official Silence
stories.summary:
Four days after a small aircraft slammed into the 109-story CITIC Tower — Beijing's tallest skyscraper — Chinese authorities have provided almost no public explanation of what happened or how it occurred. The crash, which killed the pilot and wounded 13 others, took place just a few kilometers from Zhongnanhai, the heavily guarded compound where China's top Communist Party leadership lives and works. A single 60-word statement in state-owned Beijing Daily represents the entirety of China's official public communication on the incident.

Dramatic footage of the collision has been scrubbed from Chinese social media platforms, and photographs of the tower unrelated to the crash have also been removed. At least three aviation firms confirmed to the BBC that authorities ordered a suspension of light aircraft operations following the incident, but each declined to elaborate, saying they had been instructed not to discuss it. The building, shaped like a traditional Chinese wine vessel, is a popular landmark and the broad censorship of even innocuous images of it has drawn widespread notice.

China analyst Bill Bishop described the incident as a "massive security breach," noting the aircraft came within seconds of reaching Zhongnanhai itself. Analysts say the speed and scope of the censorship response suggests Beijing's leadership may still be uncertain about exactly what happened, and that the incident threatens core government narratives about security competence. Beijing enforces a permanent no-fly zone of roughly 100 square kilometers over its political core.

The information blackout has fueled intense international speculation about whether the crash was accidental or deliberate. The opacity stands in sharp contrast to how aviation incidents are typically handled in democratic nations and underscores the difficulty of independently reporting on sensitive events inside China.
